Where it began

Scott Boland was born in Mordialloc, on the edge of Melbourne, on 11 April 1989. He played his first competitive game for Parkdale Cricket Club at the age of six, in an under-12 side, and moved to Frankston Peninsula at 16. There a coach, Nick Jewell, pushed him to take his bowling seriously, and a rookie contract with Victoria followed.

In 2017 his family learned that his grandfather, John Edward, was Aboriginal, of the Gulidjan people from around Colac. Boland set out to learn about that heritage and to play in Indigenous teams, and he became one of only a handful of Indigenous Australians to play for his country.

The player

For years he was the dependable man in Victoria's attack, helping them to Sheffield Shield titles. In 2018-19 he took 48 Shield wickets, more than any other Victorian, and was named the competition's player of the season.

His Test chance came as cover for the Ashes, and he made his debut at the MCG on 26 December 2021. In England's second innings he took six for seven. He finished that series with 18 wickets in three Tests at 9.55 and won the Mullagh Medal. Later came a winner's medal from the 2023 World Test Championship final, ten in the Sydney Test of January 2025 that won back the Border-Gavaskar Trophy, and, at Sabina Park in July 2025, a hat-trick as the West Indies were bowled out for 27. He was the first Indigenous Australian to take a Test hat-trick. By November 2026 he had 87 wickets from 20 Tests at 18.45.

What made him special

Boland was a right-arm fast-medium bowler rather than a tearaway. What he gave his captains was control: he hit his length, gave little away and broke open partnerships, as he did against India in the 2023 final when Shubman Gill, Virat Kohli and Ravindra Jadeja all fell to him in the second innings. A Test bowling average of 18.45 tells the rest.

His batting is a gentler subject. An average of 9.82 suggests nobody picked him for his strokes, although at Melbourne in the 2024-25 series he and Nathan Lyon added 56 for the last wicket to set up a famous final-day win, and his best Test score is a respectable 40.

Away from the middle

In 2018 he toured England with an Aboriginal XI marking 150 years since the first Australian sports team went overseas. His brother Nick, who played for Victoria's Future League side, was in the squad too, and it was the first time the two had ever played in the same team. Scott was named the Indigenous Cricketer of the Year by Taverners Australia. At home he also played for the Melbourne Stars.

And finally

His first one-day international for Australia, in 2016, brought nought for 74, the most expensive figures any Australian had managed on debut. Nearly six years later a commentator was suggesting they put up a statue of him. Patience, it turns out, is a fast bowler's best friend.
